objective: By the end of this lesson you can prove an airplane is airworthy for a commercial flight: find its certificates, read its inspection and AD records, check the equipment the flight needs, and handle inoperative equipment with or without an MEL.
why: As a commercial pilot you fly other people's airplanes, often for pay and with passengers or customers waiting. Extra rules apply when you fly for hire, and the pressure to go is stronger, so you need to know the rules cold and say no when the airplane is not legal.

prereading.what: Aircraft documents, inspections, MEL and inoperative equipment, preventive maintenance, special flight permits and ADs.
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 9, 9-6 to 9-13

prereading.what: How a pilot reviews the logbooks and documents before the walk-around, including the IFR checks.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 2, 2-1 to 2-4

prereading.what: Equipment for day VFR, night VFR and IFR, including the items added for flights for hire.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.205

prereading.what: Annual, 100-hour and progressive inspections, altimeter and transponder tests, and maintenance records.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.407 to 91.417

prereading.what: Inoperative instruments and equipment, with and without an MEL.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.213

prereading.what: Flying without an MEL under 91.213(d), and flying with an MEL and LOA.
prereading.label: AC 91-67A, Ch 4 and 5

warmup: A flight school asks you to fly three paying passengers on a sunset sightseeing trip in its Cessna 206. The airplane had its annual inspection 11 months ago, and the landing light is out. Name two reasons this trip may not be legal yet, even though the same airplane would be fine for a private flight in daylight.

key_terms.def: The aircraft conforms to its type design and is in condition for safe operation (14 CFR 3.5(a), as quoted in AFH 2-1).
Inspection needed every 100 hours time in service when the aircraft carries any person (not crew) for hire, or is used for flight instruction for hire by the person who provides it.
For maintenance records, the time from the moment the aircraft leaves the surface until it touches down at the next point of landing (14 CFR 1.1).
An FAA-approved inspection program that spreads the inspection over time but still inspects the whole aircraft within each 12 calendar months, in place of the annual and 100-hour.
A legally enforceable FAA rule that fixes an unsafe condition in an aircraft, engine, propeller or appliance.
Alternative method of compliance: a different way to meet an AD, usable only after the FAA office named in the AD approves it.
Special Airworthiness Information Bulletin: FAA safety information that is not regulatory, but that the FAA recommends you read and consider.
A special airworthiness certificate that lets an aircraft that does not meet airworthiness rules, but can fly safely, make a specific flight, such as to a repair shop.
Kinds of Operations Equipment List: shows which kinds of operation (VFR, IFR, day, night) the aircraft may fly and the equipment each one needs.
Minimum Equipment List for a specific aircraft plus the FAA Letter of Authorization to use it. Together they are a supplemental type certificate.
MEL symbols for a maintenance (M) or operations (O) procedure that must be done before flying with that item inoperative.

chunks.title: Who is responsible when you fly for someone else

body.p: Airworthy means the airplane matches its type design and is in condition for safe operation [[24:38|AFH 2-1]]. No one may fly a civil aircraft unless it is airworthy [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(a)]].

head: Owner or operator
You, the pilot in command
rows: Primarily responsible for keeping the aircraft airworthy, including ADs [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(a)]]
Decides if the aircraft is in condition for safe flight [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]]
Gets the required inspections done and has discrepancies repaired between them [[60:520|14 CFR 91.405(a)]]
Must discontinue the flight when unairworthy mechanical, electrical or structural conditions occur [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]]
Makes sure mechanics enter return-to-service approvals in the records [[60:521|14 CFR 91.405(b)]]
Follows the AFM/POH limitations, markings and placards [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9(a)]]

body.p: As a commercial pilot you are often not the owner. The school, company or customer keeps the records, but you still sign for the flight. Ask to see the logbooks or an airworthiness summary before you fly [[24:39|AFH 2-2]].

callout.text: If an aircraft's maintenance manual or instructions for continued airworthiness has an airworthiness limitations section, no one may fly it unless the mandatory replacement times and inspection intervals in that section have been met [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(c)]].

body.p: After maintenance, no one may fly the aircraft until a person authorized under 43.7 approves it for return to service and the record entry is made [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]]. If the work may have changed how it flies, no one other than crewmembers may ride until a pilot with at least a private certificate test-flies it and logs the flight. That means no paying passengers on that flight either [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(b)]].

check.q: The flight school's director of maintenance says the airplane is fine. Who must still decide that it is in condition for safe flight?
check.a: You, the PIC [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]]. The owner or operator keeps it maintained [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(a)]], but the go decision is yours.

chunks.title: Certificates on board: where they go and when they expire

body.p: The airplane must carry an appropriate, current airworthiness certificate [[60:485|14 CFR 91.203(a)(1)]] and an effective U.S. registration certificate [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(a)(2)]]. The airworthiness certificate must be displayed at the cabin or cockpit entrance so passengers or crew can read it [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(b)]].

head: Certificate
How long it lasts
rows: Registration (AC Form 8050-3)
Expires seven years after the last day of the month it was issued. Renew with AC Form 8050-1B during the six months before it expires [[60:168|14 CFR 47.40(a)-(b)]].
Standard airworthiness certificate (FAA Form 8100-2)
Stays in effect as long as maintenance and alterations follow Parts 21, 43 and 91 and the aircraft is registered in the U.S. [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]]
Special flight permit (FAA Form 8130-7)
Has its own expiry date, and the operating limitations issued with it (dated on the permit) are part of the certificate [[1:243|PHAK 9-13, Figure 9-10]]

body.p: Other items to find on board or on the airplane [[24:41|AFH 2-4]]:

bullets: Radio station license, for flights outside the U.S. or airplanes over 12,500 pounds (FCC rule)
Operating limitations: the FAA-approved AFM/POH, placards, instrument markings, or a mix [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9]]
Current weight and balance data
Compass correction card, if required
External data plate (14 CFR 45.11)

callout.text: Commercial trap: a fuel tank installed in the passenger or baggage compartment (common on long ferry flights) is legal only if it was installed under Part 43 and a copy of the FAA Form 337 for it is on board [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(c)]].
Logbooks are normally not kept in the airplane [[24:39|AFH 2-2]]. When you start flying for a new operator, ask where the records and the airworthiness summary live before your first trip.

check.q: A registration certificate was issued on May 6, 2026. When does it expire?
check.a: May 31, 2033: seven years after the last day of the month it was issued [[60:168|14 CFR 47.40(a)]].

chunks.title: Special airworthiness certificates and flying for hire

body.p: A standard certificate covers normal, utility, acrobatic, commuter and transport category aircraft and manned free balloons [[1:237|PHAK 9-7]]. A special certificate covers the others, such as experimental, restricted, limited, provisional and light-sport [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]]. Each special class has its own operating limits, and many of them limit flying for compensation or hire.

head: Certificate
Key limits for a commercial pilot
rows: Restricted (for example, crop dusting)

Only for its special purpose. No carrying persons or property for compensation or hire, except the people and material needed for the special purpose job. Not over densely populated areas, in a congested airway or near a busy passenger airport unless authorized [[60:507|14 CFR 91.313(a)]] [[60:508|14 CFR 91.313(c)-(e)]]
Limited

No carrying persons or property for hire in operations that need a Part 119 certificate, are listed in 119.1(e), need fractional management specifications, or are under Parts 129, 133 or 137 [[60:509|14 CFR 91.315]]
Experimental

Only for the purpose it was issued for; the same for-hire limits as limited category; tell each person carried it is experimental; VFR day only unless authorized; tell ATC it is experimental when using ATC services [[60:511|14 CFR 91.319(a), (d)]]. An experimental light-sport certificate (21.191(i), (k) or (l)) is stricter: no compensation or hire at all, except towing a light-sport glider or unpowered ultralight, or training under 91.326 [[60:511|14 CFR 91.319(e)]]
Light-sport

For compensation or hire only for glider or ultralight towing, flight training, checking and testing, or listed aerial work. Needs a condition inspection every 12 calendar months and all ADs [[60:518|14 CFR 91.327(a)-(b)]]. Towing or flight instruction for hire in a light-sport aircraft you provide also needs an inspection within the preceding 100 hours [[60:518|14 CFR 91.327(c)]]

bullets: Flight training, checking or testing in a limited or experimental aircraft generally needs a letter of deviation authority (LODA), requested at least 60 days before operations start [[60:514|14 CFR 91.326(b)]].

The annual and 100-hour rules do not apply to an aircraft with a special flight permit, a current experimental certificate, a light-sport certificate or a provisional certificate. Their own rules apply instead [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(c)(1)]].
An aircraft with an original experimental certificate may not fly with inoperative items unless its operating limitations allow it [[58:20|AC 91-67A 3.2.1]].

callout.text: Offered a paid job in an aircraft that is not standard category? Read its operating limitations first. The PHAK suggests calling the local FSDO to learn the airworthiness rules and limits of that certificate [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]].

check.q: An ag operator asks you to carry a paying sightseer in its restricted category spray plane. Can you?
check.a: No. A restricted category aircraft may not carry persons for compensation or hire, and may carry only crew and people needed for its special purpose [[60:508|14 CFR 91.313(c)-(d)]].

head: Inspection
When it is needed
Rule
rows: Annual
Within the preceding 12 calendar months, for every aircraft not excepted by 91.409(c)
100-hour
Within the preceding 100 hours time in service if the aircraft carries any person (other than a crewmember) for hire, or if you give flight instruction for hire in an aircraft you provide
Progressive
In place of the annual and 100-hour, after a written request to the Flight Standards office; must inspect the whole aircraft within each 12 calendar months

callout.text: 12 calendar months run from any day of a month to the last day of the same month the next year [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]]. Annual signed off June 3 = good through June 30 next year.

body.p: The 100-hour rule is the big change for commercial flying. Read its words closely [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]:

bullets: Carrying a person (not crew) for hire: 100-hour needed.
A school or CFI provides the airplane for paid lessons: 100-hour needed. The PHAK says it the same way: needed when the aircraft is provided by the person giving the instruction [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]].
A freelance CFI teaching in the student's own airplane: the instructor does not provide it, so this rule does not add a 100-hour. The annual still applies [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)-(b)]].
Hours are counted as time in service: from the moment the aircraft leaves the surface until it touches down at the next landing [[60:16|14 CFR 1.1]].
You may go up to 10 hours over the 100-hour limit only while en route to a place where the inspection can be done. The extra time counts toward the next 100 hours [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].
An annual may take the place of a 100-hour. A 100-hour counts as an annual only if a person authorized to do annuals does it and logs it as an annual [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]].
Who: annual by an A&P with an Inspection Authorization (IA), the manufacturer or a rated repair station; 100-hour by an A&P, a rated repair station or the manufacturer [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]].
Aircraft on an approved Part 125 or 135 inspection program, listed in the operator's operations specifications, follow that program instead [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(c)(2)]].

callout.text: If a progressive program stops, the first annual is due 12 calendar months after the last complete inspection, and the 100-hour is due 100 hours after it. A routine inspection plus a few detailed ones is not a complete inspection [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(d)]] [[60:523|14 CFR 91.409(d)]].

check.q: The school airplane's last 100-hour was at 2,300.0 hours. It is now at 2,396.5, and your paid lesson is planned for 1.5 hours. Legal?
check.a: Yes. It is due at 2,400.0, so 3.5 hours remain, enough for the 1.5-hour lesson [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].

chunks.title: ELT, transponder, altimeter and VOR checks

head: Item
Interval
Rule
rows: ELT inspection (installation, battery corrosion, controls and crash sensor, signal)
Within 12 calendar months after the last inspection
ELT battery
Replace or recharge after more than 1 cumulative hour of use, or when 50 percent of its useful life has expired; the new date goes on the ELT and in the records
Transponder
Tested and inspected within the preceding 24 calendar months before you use it
Altimeter, static system and altitude encoder
Within the preceding 24 calendar months, for IFR in controlled airspace; the static system again after it is opened (except drains and alternate static valves)
VOR receiver
Checked within the preceding 30 days to fly IFR using VOR navigation

body.p: VOR check limits and record [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)]] [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(c)-(d)]]:

bullets: VOT or repair station test signal, or a designated ground checkpoint: plus or minus 4 degrees.
Designated airborne checkpoint, or a prominent ground point on an airway centerline (preferably more than 20 NM from the VOR): plus or minus 6 degrees.
Dual VORs checked against each other on the same station: no more than 4 degrees apart.
Enter the date, place and bearing error, and sign the aircraft log or other record.

callout.text: With a VOT, center the CDI: the OBS should read 0 FROM or 180 TO [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4]]. Checkpoint and VOT locations are in the Chart Supplement [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]].

bullets: You cannot do the altimeter or transponder tests yourself. They are done by the manufacturer or a properly rated repair station; an airframe-rated mechanic may do the static system test only [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(b)]] [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413(c)]].
Do not fly IFR in controlled airspace above the highest altitude to which the altimeters and encoder were tested [[60:525|14 CFR 91.411(d)]].
Part 135 flights need an automatic-type ELT; other flights may use a personal or automatic type [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(a)]].

ELT not needed on training flights entirely within 50 NM of the departure airport, or for up to 90 days while it is out for repair with a record entry and an 'ELT not installed' placard [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)(3), (f)(10)]].
You may ferry an airplane with an inoperative ELT to a repair place, but carry only required crewmembers [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(e)]].

check.q: The transponder and altimeter checks were done in July 2024. Can you fly IFR in Class E airspace on August 2, 2026?
check.a: No. 24 calendar months from July 2024 ended July 31, 2026 [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)]]. The transponder may not be used either [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413(a)]].

body.p: Each airplane has airframe and engine logbooks, and sometimes propeller and appliance logbooks [[24:39|AFH 2-2]]. Before flight, check the logbooks or a summary of the airworthy status [[24:39|AFH 2-2]]. The AFH sample checklist below is a good model for your own summary sheet.
An inspection entry must show [[60:134|14 CFR 43.11(a)]]:

bullets: The type of inspection and a brief description of its extent
The date and the aircraft total time in service
The signature, certificate number and kind of certificate of the person approving or disapproving return to service
A statement that the aircraft was inspected and found airworthy, or that a dated list of discrepancies and unairworthy items was given to the owner or operator

head: Records the owner or operator keeps
How long
rows: Maintenance, preventive maintenance, alteration and inspection records: description, date, and the signature and certificate number of the person approving return to service
Until the work is repeated or superseded, or 1 year after the work [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(a)(1), (b)(1)]]

Total time in service; status of life-limited parts; time since overhaul; current inspection status; AD status (method, AD number and revision date, next due time and date if recurring); Form 337s for major alterations
Kept and transferred with the aircraft when sold [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(a)(2), (b)(2)]]
List of defects given after an inspection
Until the defects are repaired and the aircraft is approved for return to service [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(b)(3)]]

bullets: Items the inspector leaves inoperative under 91.213(d)(2) get an 'Inoperative' placard and go on the signed, dated discrepancy list [[60:135|14 CFR 43.11(b)]].
The owner must have those items repaired, replaced, removed or inspected at the next required inspection [[60:521|14 CFR 91.405(c)]].
Records must be shown to the FAA or the NTSB on request [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(c)]].

check.q: The last annual entry says a list of discrepancies dated March 2 was given to the owner. Is the airplane airworthy?
check.a: Not until those discrepancies are fixed and the airplane is approved for return to service, or the allowed items are properly deferred and placarded [[60:134|14 CFR 43.11(a)(5)]] [[60:135|14 CFR 43.11(b)]] [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]].

body.p: ADs are legally enforceable rules for aircraft, engines, propellers and appliances [[60:125|14 CFR 39.3]]. The FAA issues one when an unsafe condition exists and is likely to exist or develop in other products of the same type design [[60:125|14 CFR 39.5]].

bullets: Flying a product that does not meet an applicable AD is a violation, each time you operate it [[60:125|14 CFR 39.7, 39.9]].
An AD still applies if the product was modified or repaired in the area it covers [[60:125|14 CFR 39.15]].
Emergency ADs need compliance before further flight; others within a set time [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]].
Recurring ADs repeat, for example every 50 hours. There is no allowance to overfly the hour limit unless the AD says so [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]].
Anyone may propose an alternative method of compliance (AMOC) or a new compliance time. You may use it only after the manager of the office named in the AD approves it [[60:126|14 CFR 39.19]].
If an AD and the service bulletin it is based on conflict, follow the AD [[60:126|14 CFR 39.27]].
If an AD covers an item the MEL lets you defer, the AD wins: comply with the AD or an approved AMOC [[58:20|AC 91-67A 3.1.5]].

callout.text: Operators with operations specifications may have authority there to fly to a repair facility for AD work. Everyone else can ask the FSDO for a special flight permit, unless the AD says otherwise [[60:126|14 CFR 39.23]].

body.p: A Special Airworthiness Information Bulletin (SAIB) is different. It is not regulatory, but the FAA recommends that you read it and take it into account for safe flight [[1:167|PHAK 7-7]]. Example: SAIB CE-10-21 on propeller overspeed in piston airplanes [[1:167|PHAK 7-7]], and SAIB NE-11-15, which advises that 100VLL avgas is acceptable for aircraft and engines [[1:187|PHAK 7-27]].

callout.text: AD = must do (it is law). SAIB = should read (it is advice).

check.q: Your operator's mechanic wants to meet an AD with a different repair than the AD describes. When may the airplane fly with that repair?
check.a: Only after the FAA office named in the AD approves it as an alternative method of compliance [[60:126|14 CFR 39.19]].

body.p: A special flight permit is a special airworthiness certificate for an aircraft that may not meet airworthiness requirements but can fly safely [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]] [[60:78|14 CFR 21.197(a)]]. Purposes [[60:78|14 CFR 21.197(a)-(b)]]:

bullets: Fly to a base for repairs, alterations or maintenance, or to a point of storage
Deliver or export the aircraft
Production flight testing of new production aircraft
Evacuate the aircraft from an area of impending danger
Customer demonstration flights in new production aircraft that have passed production flight tests

Fly over maximum takeoff weight on flights beyond normal range over water or land without adequate landing places or fuel; the extra weight is limited to added fuel, fuel tanks and navigation equipment

body.p: How to get one:

bullets: Get help and forms from the local FSDO or a Designated Airworthiness Representative (DAR) [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]].

Submit a statement with the purpose, the proposed itinerary, the crew required, the ways the aircraft does not meet airworthiness requirements, any restrictions you think are needed for safety, and anything else the FAA needs to set operating limitations [[60:79|14 CFR 21.199(a)]].
The FAA may inspect or test the aircraft, or make you do it [[60:79|14 CFR 21.199(b)]]. The inspection is recorded in the aircraft records [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]].
The operating limitations on the permit are part of the certificate [[1:243|PHAK 9-13, Figure 9-10]]. Plan the flight around the purpose, itinerary and crew you listed, and follow every limitation.

callout.text: Commercial operators: a Part 119 certificate holder with an approved program can get a special flight permit with continuing authorization, written into its operations specifications, to fly aircraft to a maintenance base [[60:78|14 CFR 21.197(c)]] [[60:79|14 CFR 21.197(c)(1)]].

bullets: Overdue annual: a permit can get you to the inspection, but all due ADs must be done before the flight [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]].
Inoperative equipment that cannot be deferred can also be flown under a permit [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(e)]].

check.q: A hurricane is coming and the school airplane's annual ran out last week. What could let you fly it out?
check.a: A special flight permit to evacuate it from an area of impending danger [[60:78|14 CFR 21.197(a)(4)]], with all due ADs complied with [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]].

chunks.title: Preventive maintenance for a commercial pilot

body.p: Preventive maintenance is simple or minor preservation work and replacing small standard parts, with no complex assembly. Only the items listed in Part 43, Appendix A(c) count [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]] [[60:142|14 CFR Part 43 App. A(c)]].

head: Situation
May you do preventive maintenance?
rows: Airplane you own or operate, flown under Part 91
Yes, if you hold a Part 61 pilot certificate (not sport pilot) [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]]. At least a private pilot may approve it for return to service [[60:132|14 CFR 43.7(f)]].
Airplane used under Part 121, 129 or 135 (for example, your charter job)
No, not under 43.3(g) [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]]. The PHAK also says pilots may not do it on aircraft in air carrier service [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]].
Part 135 aircraft with 9 or fewer passenger seats, under the operator's FAA approval
Only removing and reinstalling approved cabin seats, stretchers and (with no tools) medical oxygen bottles, after an approved training program and written authorization [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(i)]].

bullets: Remove, install and repair landing gear tires; service shock struts; clean and grease wheel bearings
Replace bulbs, reflectors and lenses of position and landing lights; troubleshoot landing light wiring circuits
Replace or clean spark plugs and set the gap; replace hose connections (not hydraulic)
Replace any cowling that does not need prop removal or disconnecting flight controls
Clean or replace fuel and oil strainers or filters; replace and service batteries
Swap tray-mounted panel nav/com units, but not autopilots, transponders or DME, then do an operational check before use

body.p: Use the manufacturer's methods and leave the work at least equal to original condition [[60:135|14 CFR 43.13]]. Then make the record entry: a description of the work, the date completed, and your signature, certificate number and kind of certificate. Your signature approves return to service only for that work [[60:132|14 CFR 43.9(a)]].

check.q: Between charter legs under Part 135, a landing light bulb burns out. Can you, the line pilot, replace it and sign it off?
check.a: Not under 43.3(g): pilots may not do preventive maintenance on aircraft used under Part 135 [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]]. Use the operator's maintenance people.

chunks.title: Equipment for day VFR, night VFR, IFR and flights for hire

body.p: For a powered aircraft with a standard airworthiness certificate, the listed items must be installed and in operable condition for that kind of flight [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(a)]].

head: Kind of flight
Required items
Rule
rows: Day VFR

Airspeed indicator, altimeter, magnetic direction indicator, tachometer, oil pressure gauge (pressure system), temperature gauge (liquid-cooled), oil temperature gauge (air-cooled), manifold pressure gauge (altitude engine), fuel gauge for each tank, gear position indicator (retractable), anticollision lights (small airplanes certificated after March 11, 1996), seat belts, shoulder harnesses by date of manufacture, ELT if required
Day VFR, for hire, over water beyond power-off gliding distance from shore
Adds approved flotation gear readily available to each occupant and at least one pyrotechnic signaling device
Night VFR
Adds position lights, anticollision light system, an adequate source of electrical energy, and one spare set of fuses or three of each kind, accessible in flight
Night VFR, for hire
Adds one electric landing light
IFR

Day (and night, if at night) VFR items plus: two-way radio and navigation equipment suitable for the route, gyroscopic rate-of-turn indicator, slip-skid indicator, sensitive altimeter adjustable for barometric pressure, clock with hours, minutes and seconds, generator or alternator of adequate capacity, attitude indicator, heading indicator

callout.text: Study aid for IFR, built from 91.205(d): GRABCARD = Generator/alternator, Radios (comm and nav), Altimeter (sensitive), Ball (slip-skid), Clock, Attitude indicator, Rate-of-turn indicator, Directional gyro.

bullets: The rate-of-turn indicator is not required in an airplane with a third attitude instrument system installed per 121.305(j) [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(3)]].
If an anticollision light fails, you may continue to a place where it can be repaired [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(11), (c)(3)]].
WAAS GPS users flying under Part 91 are not required to carry VOR avionics [[33:70|AIM 1-1-3]]. If you do use VOR for IFR, the 30-day check applies [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)]].
91.205 is only the minimum. The AFM/POH equipment list shows what that airplane needs to be airworthy [[24:25|AFH 1-4]].

check.q: You will fly a paying passenger 15 miles off the coast, beyond power-off gliding distance from shore, in daylight. What must be added to the day VFR list?
check.a: Approved flotation gear readily available to each occupant and at least one pyrotechnic signaling device [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(12)]].

body.p: You may not take off with inoperative instruments or equipment installed unless you use an approved MEL or the 91.213(d) rule [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(a)]]. No application or approval is needed to use 91.213(d) [[58:23|AC 91-67A 4.1.1]].

callout.text: Commercial trap: 91.213(d) is only for non-turbine airplanes (and some other aircraft) [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(1)]]. Turbine-powered airplanes may not use it [[58:23|AC 91-67A 4.1.2.2]]. In a turbine single, use its MEL, fix the item, or get a special flight permit.

body.p: Step 1. The item cannot be deferred if it is [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)]]:

bullets: Part of the VFR-day type certification instruments and equipment
Shown as required on the aircraft's equipment list, or on the Kinds of Operations Equipment List (KOEL) for the flight you plan
Required by 91.205 or another Part 91 rule for that kind of flight (for example, a landing light at night for hire)
Required to be working by an AD

body.p: The KOEL lists the kinds of operations (VFR, IFR, day, night) the aircraft can fly and the equipment that affects them. It has no standard format, so the maker may show it in different ways. An item the KOEL requires for that operation may not be deferred [[58:9|AC 91-67A 1.8.9]].
Step 2. If it is none of those [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)-(4)]]:

bullets: Remove it (cockpit control placarded, maintenance recorded per 43.9), or deactivate it and placard it 'Inoperative'. Deactivation that involves maintenance is done and recorded under Part 43.
A certificated, appropriately rated pilot or maintenance person decides the item is not a hazard to the aircraft.

head: Action
AC 91-67A guidance
rows: Removal
An authorized person records it per 43.9, adjusts weight and balance and the equipment list if needed, placards the controls, and files a Form 337 if appropriate [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.1]]
Deactivation
Turning off a switch does not remove power. Deactivation is not preventive maintenance; an authorized person does it and makes the 43.9 entry [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]]
Placard
Legible, visible to the crew, next to the control or indicator, not covering other controls [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.3]]

bullets: Deferrals are for problems found before flight. In flight, use the AFM/POH procedures [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]].
Deferred items must be repaired, replaced, removed or inspected at the next required inspection [[60:521|14 CFR 91.405(c)]].

check.q: You plan night VFR, not IFR. The KOEL shows the attitude indicator required only for IFR, and it has failed. Can it be deferred for tonight's flight?
check.a: Possibly. It is not on the 91.205 night VFR list [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)]], and the KOEL requires it only for IFR [[58:9|AC 91-67A 1.8.9]]. If the equipment list and ADs do not require it, have it deactivated and placarded, and decide it is not a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]].

body.p: There are three ways to fly with inoperative equipment: an MEL with an LOA, the 91.213(d) rule, or a special flight permit [[58:20|AC 91-67A 3.2]]. To use an MEL, all of these must be true [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(a)]]:

bullets: An approved MEL exists for that aircraft.
A Letter of Authorization (LOA) is in the aircraft. The MEL and LOA together are a supplemental type certificate.
The aircraft records available to you describe the inoperative items.
You follow every condition and limit in the MEL and the LOA.

body.p: Reading the sample: item 2 may be inoperative if the flight does not depend on that system. Item 4 has an (O): an operations procedure (verify the manual drain valve is closed) must be done before flight. An (M) means a maintenance procedure [[58:10|AC 91-67A 1.8.11]] [[58:11|AC 91-67A 1.8.18]]. The operator's MEL may be more restrictive than the master MEL (MMEL), never less [[58:10|AC 91-67A 1.8.13]].

bullets: Once an LOA is issued, using the MEL is mandatory for that aircraft [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].
If you are authorized to use an MEL issued under Part 91K, 121, 125 or 135, you must use it on Part 91 flights too [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(c)]] [[58:21|AC 91-67A 3.4]].

LOAs go to the operator with operational control. A lessee in a dry lease may not use the lessor's MEL and needs its own LOA [[58:21|AC 91-67A 3.3.3]]. Part 141 pilot schools can also hold MEL LOAs [[58:9|AC 91-67A 1.8.10]].
The MEL and LOA must be accessible to the PIC, in print or digital. Telephone, radio or data link access is not acceptable [[58:27|AC 91-67A 5.1]].

MEL relief applies up to takeoff, when you begin applying takeoff power. A failure after takeoff is handled with the AFM/POH, recorded, and repaired or deferred before the next takeoff [[58:27|AC 91-67A 5.1.1, 5.1.3]].
A means of recording discrepancies must be in the aircraft. If a separate discrepancy log is used, it is kept as part of the aircraft records [[58:28|AC 91-67A 5.2]].

An MEL may not include items required by the type certification rules and essential for safety, items an AD requires, or items Part 91 requires for that operation [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(b)]]. Items not listed as deferrable (for example tachometer, flaps, stall warning) must be fixed or flown under a special flight permit [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

check.q: The MEL item for a failed system has an (M) in the remarks column. Can you take off as soon as you placard it?
check.a: No. The (M) maintenance procedure must be done before operating with the item inoperative [[58:28|AC 91-67A 5.4.1]], and takeoff is not allowed until the deferral process is complete [[58:27|AC 91-67A 5.1.2]].

chunks.title: Risk: inoperative equipment found before flight

body.p: Legal is not the same as safe. Inoperative equipment is an aircraft ('A') hazard. An inoperative landing light can make night flight more hazardous even when the rule does not require one. Weigh each item against the conditions you expect [[30:25|RMH 3-7]].
Before flying with an inoperative item, with or without an MEL, the FAA says to check [[58:25|AC 91-67A 4.4]] [[58:27|AC 91-67A 5.1.4]]:

bullets: That the item, and how it failed, is not a hazard to the operation
That it is not needed for the planned flight (for example oceanic, remote or international)
How several failures add up
Weather, night, the departure and destination airports, the en route environment, and diversion options
Extra workload, crew fatigue and other human factors

callout.text: External pressure ('E') is strongest in commercial flying: business reasons, customers waiting, not wanting to disappoint someone. Pilots under pressure sometimes fail to consider the other hazards [[30:26|RMH 3-8]]. Decide on airworthiness before the passengers arrive.

bullets: Redundancy matters more at night or in IMC. One radio may be fine for day VFR but is a hazard in IMC [[30:24|RMH 3-6]].
Do not defer lightly, especially if other items are already inoperative [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].
When the plan changes (day to night, VFR to IFR, private to for hire), check the item again for the new kind of flight [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(ii)-(iii)]].

check.q: Your deferred, placarded #2 comm radio was fine for a VFR leg. The return leg is now IFR in clouds. What should you do?
check.a: Re-check whether it is required for IFR on the equipment list or KOEL [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(ii)]], and weigh the loss of redundancy in IMC [[30:24|RMH 3-6]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: the checkride airworthiness review

body.p: Expect the examiner to hand you the logbooks and a commercial scenario (often for hire, at night or IFR). Work in this order:

bullets: 1. Documents: show the displayed airworthiness certificate and the registration and say when each expires [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203]] [[60:168|14 CFR 47.40]]. Show the AFM/POH, weight and balance, and equipment list [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].
2. Inspections: last annual and its last legal day; the 100-hour and hours remaining if the flight is for hire [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409]].
3. Other checks: ELT and battery date, transponder; and for IFR, altimeter/static/encoder and the VOR check [[24:40|AFH 2-3]].
4. ADs: show the AD status record and any recurring AD's next due time [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(a)(2)(v)]].
5. Equipment: name what 91.205 needs for this flight, including the for-hire items [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(12), (c)(4)]].
6. Inoperative item: say MEL or 91.213(d), walk through the steps out loud, then decide: fix, defer or cancel [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]].
7. Risk: say how the item changes your plan, and what pressure you feel to go [[30:25|RMH 3-7]].

callout.text: Examiners like to change one fact at a time: day to night, private to for hire, VFR to IFR, piston to turbine. Each change can add equipment, inspections or remove the 91.213(d) option.

check.q: The examiner changes the trip from a private flight to one carrying a paying passenger. Which logbook item do you now look for?
check.a: A 100-hour (or annual) inspection within the preceding 100 hours time in service [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].

scenario.title: The sunset sightseeing trip
scenario.setup: Today is October 20, 2026. You are a new commercial pilot at a flight school that holds the operating approvals it needs for this trip. You will fly three paying passengers in its Cessna 206 (non-turbine, no MEL), leaving at 4 p.m. and landing back after sunset. You hoped to file IFR for the return because low clouds may move in. The logbooks show: annual signed off November 14, 2025; last 100-hour at 3,204.6 hours time in service, and the airplane is now at 3,297.9; transponder test February 2025; altimeter, static and encoder test September 2024. The trip is planned at 3.1 hours. On preflight, the landing light does not work and the #2 comm radio is dead.

questions.q: Are the annual and 100-hour current for this trip?
questions.a: Yes. The annual is good through November 30, 2026 [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]] [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]]. The 100-hour is due at 3,304.6, so 6.7 hours remain, enough for 3.1 hours [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]. Do not plan on the 10-hour allowance: it is only for flying to a place where the inspection can be done [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].

questions.q: Can you file IFR for the return?
questions.a: Not in controlled airspace. The altimeter, static and encoder test from September 2024 ran out at the end of September 2026 [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)]]. The transponder test from February 2025 is still good through February 2027 [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413(a)]]. Plan a VFR return or change the trip.

questions.q: Can you defer the landing light under 91.213(d)?
questions.a: No. One electric landing light is required at night for hire [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(4)]], and items 91.205 requires for that kind of flight cannot be deferred [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]]. Under Part 91 you may replace the bulb yourself as preventive maintenance, if the school allows it [[60:142|App. A(c)(17)]] [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]], approve it [[60:132|14 CFR 43.7(f)]] and log it [[60:132|14 CFR 43.9(a)]]. Or have a mechanic fix it, or be back before sunset.

questions.q: What about the dead #2 comm radio?
questions.a: 91.205 does not require it for VFR [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)]]. If the equipment list, KOEL and ADs do not require it, it may be deferred: an authorized person deactivates it and makes the 43.9 entry [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]], it is placarded 'Inoperative', and a rated pilot or mechanic decides it is not a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)-(4)]].

questions.q: The passengers have paid and are watching the sky. How should risk shape your decision?
questions.a: Business pressure and people waiting are 'E' hazards that make pilots overlook other hazards [[30:26|RMH 3-8]]. Count the stack: night, a possible low ceiling, no IFR option, one comm radio [[58:25|AC 91-67A 4.4]] [[30:24|RMH 3-6]]. A reasonable choice is to fly earlier and land before sunset, or to reschedule.

skills.do: Find the airworthiness and registration certificates, explain where each must be and when each expires, and point out the operating limitations, weight and balance data, equipment list and data plate. Explain what changes for a special airworthiness certificate.
skills.practice: In each airplane you fly for hire, find every item on the AFH 2-4 document list and say the rule for each [[24:41|AFH 2-4]]. Practice the registration expiry math with real certificates [[60:168|14 CFR 47.40]].

skills.do: In the examiner's scenario (for hire, night or IFR), use the logbooks to show annual, 100-hour, ELT, transponder, altimeter/static, VOR check and AD status, and decide if the airplane is airworthy for that flight.
skills.practice: Build a one-page airworthiness summary like AFH Figure 2-4 for your school's airplanes, with real due dates and hours remaining [[24:40|AFH 2-3]]. Update it after every inspection.

skills.do: Given an inoperative item, decide if the airplane uses an MEL or 91.213(d), check the equipment list, KOEL, 91.205 and ADs, say who deactivates and placards it and what is recorded, or choose to fix it, get a special flight permit or cancel.
skills.practice: Have your CFI name broken items (landing light, attitude indicator, #2 radio, fuel gauge) and change the flight: day or night, VFR or IFR, private or for hire, piston or turbine. Talk through 91.213 each time [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213]] [[58:23|AC 91-67A Ch 4]].

quiz.q: A flight school provides both the airplane and the instructor for paid lessons. Beyond the annual, which inspection does this add?
options: A progressive inspection every 50 hours
A 100-hour inspection
A new airworthiness certificate each year
A 30-day VOR check before every lesson
quiz.why: No one may give flight instruction for hire in an aircraft that person provides unless it had an annual or 100-hour within the preceding 100 hours time in service [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].

quiz.q: Which aircraft may NOT use the 91.213(d) no-MEL deferral rule?
options: A non-turbine small airplane with no MMEL
A non-turbine small airplane with an MMEL
A turbine-powered airplane
A glider
quiz.why: 91.213(d)(1) lists non-turbine airplanes, rotorcraft, gliders and some others [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(1)]]. AC 91-67A says turbine-powered airplanes may not use 91.213(d) [[58:23|AC 91-67A 4.1.2.2]].

quiz.q: Using a designated VOR checkpoint on the airport surface, what is the largest bearing error allowed for IFR?
options: Plus or minus 4 degrees
Plus or minus 6 degrees
Plus or minus 2 degrees
Plus or minus 10 degrees
quiz.why: A ground checkpoint or a VOT allows plus or minus 4 degrees; an airborne checkpoint allows 6 [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)]].

quiz.q: For night VFR, which item does 91.205 add only when the flight is for hire?
options: Position lights
An anticollision light system
Spare fuses accessible in flight
One electric landing light
quiz.why: One electric landing light is required if the aircraft is operated for hire [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(4)]]. The others are required on every night VFR flight.

quiz.q: What does a Kinds of Operations Equipment List (KOEL) tell you?
options: Which items an MEL lets you defer
The kinds of operations the aircraft can fly and the equipment that affects them
Which ADs apply to the airplane
The weight and arm of each installed item
quiz.why: The KOEL specifies the kinds of operations (VFR, IFR, day, night) and the installed equipment that may affect any operating limitation [[58:9|AC 91-67A 1.8.9]].

quiz.q: Which statement about a Special Airworthiness Information Bulletin (SAIB) is correct?
options: It requires compliance before further flight
It replaces the AD it is based on
It is not regulatory, but the FAA recommends you read and consider it
It applies only to experimental aircraft
quiz.why: Although a SAIB is not regulatory in nature, the FAA recommends that the information be read and taken into consideration [[1:167|PHAK 7-7]]. An emergency AD is the one that needs compliance before further flight [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]].

quiz.q: You fly a Part 135 operator's airplane. Under 43.3(g), what preventive maintenance may you do on it?
options: Any item on the Appendix A(c) list
Only light bulbs and tires
Any item, if you hold a commercial certificate
None under 43.3(g), because the aircraft is used under Part 135
quiz.why: 43.3(g) covers aircraft owned or operated by the pilot that are not used under Part 121, 129 or 135 [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]]. A separate 135 approval can allow pilots to remove and reinstall cabin seats [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(i)]].

quiz.q: Your airplane has an MEL and LOA. When does MEL relief stop applying to a newly found inoperative item?
options: When you begin applying power for takeoff
When you start the engine
When you call for taxi
When you reach cruise altitude
quiz.why: MEL relief may be applied up until takeoff, the point where the pilot begins to apply power to start the takeoff. Failures after takeoff are handled with the AFM/POH [[58:27|AC 91-67A 5.1.1, 5.1.3]].

quiz.q: Which is a listed purpose for a special flight permit?
options: Carrying paying passengers in an airplane with an overdue annual
Flight training in an airplane with an open AD
Flying the aircraft to a base where repairs will be done
IFR flight with an expired altimeter test
quiz.why: Purposes include flying to a base for repairs, alterations or maintenance, delivery or export, production flight tests, evacuation from danger, and customer demonstrations [[60:78|14 CFR 21.197(a)]].

quiz.q: A crop duster has a restricted category certificate. What may it carry?
options: Paying passengers on short local flights
Flight crew and people needed for its special purpose job
Any cargo for hire, as long as no passengers are aboard
Anyone, if the pilot holds a commercial certificate
quiz.why: Only crewmembers, crew trainees and people needed for the special purpose may be carried, and no persons or property for compensation or hire outside that purpose [[60:508|14 CFR 91.313(c)-(d)]].

takeaways: You decide if the airplane is safe to fly, even when the owner or operator does the maintenance [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7]].
Flying for hire adds a 100-hour inspection, a landing light at night, and flotation gear over water beyond gliding distance [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]] [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205]].
For IFR: altimeter, static and encoder within 24 calendar months, VOR check within 30 days when using VOR, and the 91.205(d) equipment [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411]] [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171]].
ADs are law; SAIBs are advice. AMOCs need FAA approval first [[60:125|14 CFR 39.7]] [[1:167|PHAK 7-7]] [[60:126|14 CFR 39.19]].
No preventive maintenance by pilots on aircraft used under Part 135 [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]].
Turbine airplanes cannot use 91.213(d); with an LOA, the MEL is mandatory [[58:23|AC 91-67A 4.1.2.2]] [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].
Legal is not always safe, and business pressure makes it harder to see [[30:26|RMH 3-8]].
cfi_notes: Drill the 100-hour wording: persons (not crew) for hire, or instruction for hire in an aircraft the instructor provides. Students often think every commercial flight needs it, or that a CFI teaching in a student's own airplane needs it.
Common error: thinking the 10-hour overfly lets you finish a paid trip. It is only for reaching a place where the inspection can be done, and the hours count toward the next 100.
Examiners love to switch one fact: day to night, private to for hire, VFR to IFR, piston to turbine. Make the student re-run 91.205 and 91.213 each time.

Preventive maintenance: 43.3(g) allows Part 61 pilots (not sport) to do it, and 43.7(f) needs at least a private pilot to approve it. PHAK 9-12 says student and recreational pilots are excluded entirely; teach the regulation. For commercial students stress the Part 121/129/135 exclusion.

Deactivation: PHAK 9-10 says a pilot may simply pull a circuit breaker. AC 91-67A 4.2.2 says deactivation is not preventive maintenance, a switch does not remove power, and an authorized person must do it and make the 43.9 entry. Teach the AC and the operator's procedure.

Pink copy of the registration application: PHAK 9-7 says 90 days; current 47.31(c) has no day limit (valid inside the U.S. until the certificate arrives or the application is denied). Teach the regulation.
PHAK 9-10 refers to AC 91-67, which was canceled on November 3, 2017 [[58:6|AC 91-67A 1.4]]. Use AC 91-67A.
The only MEL sample in these sources is a helicopter MMEL page (IPH Figure 7-6). Use it to teach the columns and the (O) symbol, not the helicopter items.
gaps: Which for-hire operations a commercial pilot may conduct under Part 91 versus Parts 119/135 (for example 119.1(e)) is not covered in the provided sources; the lesson tells students to confirm the operator holds the needed approvals.
SAIBs are described only briefly in PHAK 7-7 and 7-27 (not regulatory, FAA recommends reading); how to search for them is not in the provided sources (K1c).
No sample KOEL is in the resources. AC 91-67A 1.8.9 explains what a KOEL is and that it has no standard format (K3c).
No airplane MEL sample is in the resources; the IPH sample is a helicopter MMEL page (K3b).
GRABCARD is a study aid built from 91.205(d); the acronym itself is not in the FAA resources. Multiengine-only items (such as 91.409(e) turbine multiengine inspection programs) are not taught.

activities.title: Work out the due times
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: The school's airplane had its last 100-hour at 2,861.4 hours time in service. It is now at 2,948.9. How many hours remain before the next 100-hour is due?
A 100-hour was due at 3,100.0. The airplane flew 6.2 hours over to reach a shop and was inspected at 3,106.2. At what time in service is the next 100-hour due?
items.why: The excess time used to reach the shop counts toward the next 100 hours, so it is due at 3,100.0 + 100 = 3,200.0, not 3,306.2 [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].

items.q: Dual VOR check: both receivers are tuned to the same station. VOR 1 shows 274 degrees and VOR 2 shows 279 degrees. How many degrees apart are they?
items.why: 279 - 274 = 5 degrees. The limit is 4, so this check fails; do not fly IFR using VOR until it is fixed [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(c)]].

items.q: At a ground checkpoint designated for the 180 radial, your CDI centers with the OBS on 176 FROM. What is the bearing error in degrees?
items.why: 180 - 176 = 4 degrees, right at the plus or minus 4 degree limit for a ground checkpoint, so it passes. Log the date, place and bearing error and sign [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(2)]] [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].

items.q: An ELT battery has a manufacturer's useful life of 4 years and the ELT has never been used. After how many years must it be replaced?
items.why: Replace it when 50 percent of its useful life has expired: 50 percent of 4 years = 2 years (or sooner after more than 1 cumulative hour of use) [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]].

activities.title: Match the check to its interval
activities.intro: Tap a check, then the rule that goes with it.

pairs.r: Within 30 days, when using VOR for IFR
24 calendar months, for IFR in controlled airspace
24 calendar months, before you use it
12 calendar months after the last one
Every 100 hours when carrying persons for hire
Retest before IFR in controlled airspace

activities.title: True or false: ADs, permits and pilot maintenance
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: As a pilot for a Part 135 operator, you may clean the spark plugs on the company airplane under 43.3(g).
cards.why: 43.3(g) does not cover aircraft used under Part 121, 129 or 135 [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]].

cards.s: A SAIB is regulatory, so you must comply before further flight.
cards.why: A SAIB is not regulatory; the FAA recommends reading and considering it [[1:167|PHAK 7-7]].

cards.s: If you cannot meet an AD as written, you may propose an alternative method of compliance and use it once the FAA approves it.
cards.why: Anyone may propose an AMOC, and may use it only if the manager of the office named in the AD approves it [[60:126|14 CFR 39.19]].

cards.s: A Part 119 certificate holder can have a special flight permit with continuing authorization in its operations specifications.
cards.why: 21.197(c) allows a continuing authorization, set out in the certificate holder's operations specifications, for flights to a maintenance base [[60:78|14 CFR 21.197(c)]] [[60:79|14 CFR 21.197(c)(1)]].

cards.s: Swapping a tray-mounted panel transponder is preventive maintenance.
cards.why: The tray-mounted avionics item excludes autopilots, transponders and DME [[60:143|App. A(c)(31)]].

cards.s: An aircraft flying under a special flight permit does not need a current annual for that flight.
cards.why: The annual and 100-hour rules do not apply to an aircraft that carries a special flight permit [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(c)(1)]].

activities.title: What does this flight add?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: Oil temperature gauge for an air-cooled engine
One electric landing light at night
Flotation gear beyond power-off gliding distance from shore
Clock showing hours, minutes and seconds
Sensitive altimeter adjustable for barometric pressure

activities.title: Read the equipment list
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin. Use the key at the top of the list.

activities.title: Defer an item with an MEL
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Find the inoperative item before takeoff
Make an entry in the maintenance or discrepancy record
Confirm in the MEL that the item may be inoperative for this flight
Do the required (M) or (O) procedure, such as opening the circuit breaker
Take off and follow the MEL conditions and limits

activities.title: The evening charter that almost went
activities.intro: You are flying N4471K, a non-turbine Cessna 182 with no MEL, for a flight school that holds the approvals it needs. Two paying passengers are booked on a local flight that lands 40 minutes after sunset. You start your airworthiness review an hour before departure.

steps.s: The last 100-hour was at 4,512.3 hours time in service. The airplane is at 4,609.8, and the flight is planned at 1.5 hours. What do you decide?
options: Ground it: a new 100-hour is needed first
Fly: 2.5 hours remain before the 100-hour is due
Fly: you may go 10 hours over the 100-hour anyway
Fly: the 100-hour does not apply when the annual is current
steps.why: Due at 4,612.3; 4,612.3 - 4,609.8 = 2.5 hours, enough for 1.5 [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]. The 10-hour allowance is only for reaching an inspection [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].

steps.s: On preflight, the landing light bulb is burned out. The school lets pilots replace bulbs. What now?
options: Placard it INOPERATIVE and go, since only position lights are needed at night
Go, because the anticollision lights are enough
Replace the bulb, and log the work, date, your signature, certificate number and kind
Ask the FSDO for a special flight permit for the passenger flight
steps.why: A landing light is required at night for hire, so it cannot be deferred [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(4)]] [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]]. Replacing the bulb is preventive maintenance a pilot may do under Part 91 and log [[60:142|App. A(c)(17)]] [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]] [[60:132|14 CFR 43.9(a)]].

steps.s: Next you find the #2 nav/com radio dead. It is not on the 91.205 VFR list, and the equipment list, KOEL and ADs do not require it. What is the right way to defer it?
options: Pull its circuit breaker yourself and go, with no entry
Cancel, because every installed item must work
Write 'INOP' on the passenger manifest only
Have an authorized person deactivate it and log it, placard it, and decide it is not a hazard
steps.why: Without an MEL, it must be deactivated and placarded 'Inoperative' and judged not a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)-(4)]]. AC 91-67A says an authorized person deactivates it and makes the 43.9 entry [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]].

steps.s: After sunset on the way back, the ammeter shows a discharge and the alternator light comes on. What do you do?
options: Follow the AFM/POH procedure, reduce the electrical load, and land as soon as practical
Continue the planned tour, since the battery is still powering the lights
Defer the alternator under 91.213(d) and continue
Turn off all lights to save the battery and finish the tour
steps.why: Deferrals are not for in-flight failures; use the AFM/POH procedures [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. The PIC must discontinue the flight when unairworthy electrical conditions occur [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]], and night VFR needs an adequate source of electrical energy [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(5)]].

final_quiz.q: An annual inspection was signed off on August 9, 2025. On which date is the airplane first overdue?
options: August 9, 2026
August 10, 2026
September 1, 2026
August 31, 2026
final_quiz.why: 12 calendar months run to the last day of the same month the next year, so it is good through August 31, 2026 and overdue on September 1, 2026 [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]] [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]].

final_quiz.q: The last 100-hour was at 1,450.0 hours. The airplane is at 1,553.0, at its home base where the shop is. Can you fly a paying passenger on a 0.8-hour trip first?
options: Yes, you may go up to 10 hours over
Yes, if the annual is current
No, it is overdue, and the 10-hour allowance is only for reaching a place to do the inspection
No, but you may fly the passenger if you log the overflight
final_quiz.why: It was due at 1,550.0. The limit may be exceeded by not more than 10 hours only while en route to reach a place where the inspection can be done [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].

final_quiz.q: The altimeter, static and encoder test was done in March 2024. On April 3, 2026, may you file and fly IFR in Class E airspace?
options: No, the test ran out at the end of March 2026
Yes, the test is good for 36 calendar months
Yes, if the VOR check is current
Yes, as long as you stay below 10,000 feet
final_quiz.why: IFR in controlled airspace needs the test within the preceding 24 calendar months; March 2024 runs through March 31, 2026 [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)]].

final_quiz.q: You do an airborne VOR check over a prominent ground point on an airway centerline. What is the largest error allowed, and what must you record?
options: 4 degrees; the date and your initials
6 degrees; the date, place, bearing error and your signature
6 degrees; nothing, if the error is within limits
10 degrees; the radial used and the aircraft hours
final_quiz.why: The maximum variation is 6 degrees for this check [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(b)(4)(iii)]], and you enter the date, place and bearing error and sign the aircraft log or other record [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].

final_quiz.q: You fly your employer's Part 135 airplane on a Part 91 positioning flight. A cabin reading light is inoperative. How do you handle it?
options: Use 91.213(d), since this leg is under Part 91
Ignore it, since cabin lights are not on 91.205
Get a special flight permit for every positioning leg
Use the company's approved MEL
final_quiz.why: A person authorized to use an MEL issued under Part 135 must use that MEL to comply with 91.213 [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(c)]] [[58:21|AC 91-67A 3.4]].

final_quiz.q: You dry-lease an airplane from an owner whose MEL and LOA are on board. Can you defer items with that MEL?
options: Yes, the MEL goes with the airplane
No, you need an LOA issued to you as the operator
Yes, if the owner gives you written permission
No, MELs are only for Part 135
final_quiz.why: LOAs are issued to the operator exercising operational control. In a dry lease the lessee is the operator and may use only an MEL LOA issued to them [[58:21|AC 91-67A 3.3.3]].

final_quiz.q: A recurring AD on your propeller is due every 100 hours. It was last done at 812.4 hours, and the airplane is at 905.0. How many hours may you fly before it is due?
options: 17.4 hours
7.4 hours
10 hours plus the time to reach a shop
92.6 hours
final_quiz.why: Next due at 812.4 + 100 = 912.4; 912.4 - 905.0 = 7.4 hours. There is no provision to overfly an AD's hour limit unless the AD says so [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]] [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(a)(2)(v)]].

final_quiz.q: In cruise on an MEL-equipped airplane, a nav radio fails. What does the guidance say?
options: Defer it in flight using the MEL
Placard it and keep flying for the rest of the day
Use the AFM/POH, record the failure, and repair or defer it before the next takeoff
Land immediately at the nearest airport in every case
final_quiz.why: MEL relief does not apply to failures after takeoff. Use the AFM/POH, record the failure, and repair it or follow the MEL deferral before the next takeoff [[58:27|AC 91-67A 5.1.3]].

final_quiz.q: You will carry paying passengers over a lake, beyond power-off gliding distance from shore, in daylight. What equipment is added?
options: Flotation gear for each occupant and at least one pyrotechnic signaling device
A second comm radio and a landing light
An automatic ELT and a life raft
Nothing, if you stay within 50 NM of the departure airport
final_quiz.why: For hire over water beyond power-off gliding distance from shore: approved flotation gear readily available to each occupant and at least one pyrotechnic signaling device [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(12)]].

final_quiz.q: A customer offers to pay you to fly passengers in his experimental airplane on a trip that would require a Part 119 certificate. What is true?
options: It is legal if you hold a commercial certificate
It is legal in VFR day conditions
It is legal if you tell each passenger it is experimental
It is not allowed in an experimental aircraft
final_quiz.why: No person may operate an experimental aircraft carrying persons or property for compensation or hire in operations that require a Part 119 certificate [[60:511|14 CFR 91.319(a)(2)(i)]].

final_quiz.q: During an annual, the IA finds the autopilot inoperative and it may be left inoperative under 91.213(d)(2). What must the IA do?
options: Remove it and file a Form 337
Placard it 'Inoperative' and add it to the signed, dated discrepancy list
Note it only in the pilot's logbook
Ground the airplane until it is repaired
final_quiz.why: For items permitted to be inoperative under 91.213(d)(2), the inspector placards each one 'Inoperative' and adds it to the signed and dated list of discrepancies given to the owner [[60:135|14 CFR 43.11(b)]].

final_quiz.q: You ferry an airplane with an inoperative ELT from a field with no shop to one that can fix it. Who may ride along?
options: Only required crewmembers
Up to two passengers who are not paying
Anyone, if you stay within 50 NM
Anyone, if the ELT is placarded
final_quiz.why: No person other than required crewmembers may be carried on an airplane ferried under 91.207(e) [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(e)]].

final_quiz.q: A mechanic re-rigged the flight controls on the school's airplane. Before you take paying passengers, what is needed?
options: Only the mechanic's return-to-service entry
A new airworthiness certificate
A test flight by a pilot with at least a private certificate, with an operational check logged in the aircraft records
A special flight permit for the first flight
final_quiz.why: If maintenance may have appreciably changed flight characteristics, no one other than crew may be carried until a pilot with at least a private certificate flies it, checks the work and logs the flight [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(b)]], unless ground tests show conclusively it did not [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(c)]].
